questions.stem: You are examining the feet of Jack, 57, at his annual diabetes review in general practice. He reports a year of numb toes, "like I'm wearing socks". You now test protective sensation with a 10 g monofilament at standard sites on each foot. Which technique is correct?
options: Press firmly over any callus, as these sites carry the highest plantar pressure
Apply perpendicular to the skin until it bends, hold 1 to 2 seconds, with his eyes closed
Drag the filament lightly along the sole and ask whether he feels it scratch
Demonstrate on his toe first, then test each site while he watches the filament
questions.why: The 10 g monofilament is pressed at right angles until it buckles, which delivers a fixed 10 g force. It is held about 1 to 2 seconds while the patient's eyes are closed, after a demonstration on the hand or sternum. If he cannot feel it, he has lost protective sensation.
notes: Callus dampens sensation and gives a false negative, so test next to callus, scar or ulcer and never over it.
Dragging tests a different stimulus with no set force, so the result cannot be read as loss of protective sensation.
Show him the feel on a sensate area such as the hand, not the foot being tested, and keep his eyes closed so he cannot guess from sight.

questions.stem: Jack, 57, takes metformin XR 2 g and glargine 30 units nightly, injected into the same thigh site, which has lipohypertrophy. HbA1c is 9.4% (79 mmol/mol), eGFR 76 and uACR 6.8 mg/mmol. He has had two mild hypos when he skipped lunch. Along with fixing his injection technique, which is the best glucose-lowering change to make now?
options: Add gliclazide MR 30 mg orally once daily with breakfast
Add empagliflozin 10 mg orally once daily
Add sitagliptin 100 mg orally once daily
Increase glargine to 36 units subcutaneously at night
questions.why: With albuminuria (early diabetic kidney disease) and high cardiovascular risk, an SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred because it protects the kidneys and heart independently of glucose lowering. Consider reducing glargine and give sick-day advice (ketoacidosis risk).
notes: A sulfonylurea on top of insulin makes hypos more likely in a man who already has them, and it does not protect the kidneys or heart.
A DPP-4 inhibitor lowers HbA1c only modestly and has no proven kidney or cardiovascular benefit, so it is not preferred with albuminuria.
Raising the dose while he injects into lipohypertrophy and is already having hypos risks severe hypos once he moves to healthy skin.

questions.stem: Jack, 57, has type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 76 and a uACR of 6.8 mg/mmol. You start an SGLT2 inhibitor, partly to slow his kidney disease, and warn him that his eGFR may dip a little at first. By what mechanism does this drug lower intraglomerular pressure?
options: It dilates the efferent arteriole by blocking the action of angiotensin II
It lowers glucose, reducing glycation of the glomerular basement membrane
It raises sodium delivery to the macula densa, restoring afferent arteriolar constriction
It blocks aldosterone in the collecting duct, reducing sodium reabsorption
questions.why: In diabetes, increased proximal sodium-glucose reabsorption means less sodium reaches the macula densa, so the afferent arteriole dilates and the glomerulus hyperfilters. SGLT2 blockade restores tubuloglomerular feedback, which constricts the afferent arteriole and lowers glomerular pressure.
notes: Efferent arteriolar dilation is how ACE inhibitors and ARBs such as his perindopril work, not SGLT2 inhibitors.
The kidney benefit appears quickly and does not depend on glucose lowering, so long-term glycation is not the main mechanism.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or finerenone work this way; SGLT2 inhibitors act in the proximal tubule.

questions.stem: Jack, 57, smokes, has diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and has stocking sensory loss in both feet. During his foot examination you assess for peripheral arterial disease and go to palpate the dorsalis pedis pulse. Where on the foot is this pulse best felt?
options: Behind the medial malleolus, between it and the calcaneal tendon
On the dorsum of the foot, just medial to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
In front of the lateral malleolus, over the sinus tarsi
On the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon
questions.why: The dorsalis pedis artery continues from the anterior tibial artery and runs on the dorsum just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, towards the proximal first intermetatarsal space. Ask the patient to extend the big toe to find the tendon.
notes: That is where you feel the posterior tibial pulse, the other foot pulse to check in this examination.
The artery runs lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, not medial to it.
Nothing large enough to palpate runs over the sinus tarsi; the dorsalis pedis is on the dorsum, well medial to this.
